rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient covering almost the full organic range at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and reveal the usable elution window. The moderate gradient time balances seeing retention/selectivity patterns against avoiding an unnecessarily truncated first run.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only improvement is to cut t_last below 10 min by trimming the gradient to the observed elution window and making it steeper. The first peak is well retained, so raising phi0 and lowering phi1 should compress the run while likely preserving adequate resolution.

We only need to shave about 0.4 min from the last peak while keeping the weakest pair above 1.5, so a modest increase in temperature plus a slightly steeper gradient should shorten the run enough without sacrificing full resolution. I raised phi1 slightly to keep the last compound inside the gradient while maintaining a compressed window.

The collapse of pair 6/7 at higher temperature shows this is mainly a temperature-sensitive selectivity problem, not just slope, so move cooler than the successful 40 C run while keeping a somewhat steeper gradient to try to bring t_last under 10 min. This tests whether lower T restores that critical pair while the shorter tG still trims enough time.

Compared with the 10 min run, shortening to 8 min at 35 C mainly hurt the 5/6 pair, while raising to 45 C collapsed 6/7, so 40 C appears near the selectivity sweet spot. Repeating the successful phi window at 8 min tests whether the critical pairs still stay above 1.5 while bringing the last peak below 10 min, which would improve on the current best.

The last peak is already comfortably before 10 min, so the only path to a higher CRF is restoring full credit to the 6/7 pair without changing temperature away from the best selectivity seen so far. Narrowing the window slightly at the top should shallow the effective gradient in the crowded middle/late region and may increase the weakest resolution while keeping all compounds inside the gradient.

A different nearby optimum is worth probing: lowering phi1 one more step may pull the final compound slightly later but can further shallow the effective gradient in the crowded region and preserve or improve the weakest pair. Since 1.000 is already achieved, this is only to map robustness around the optimum with a genuinely different method.

The current best is already maximal, so this different run should probe robustness from the other direction: slightly longer tG will tend to help the critical 6/7 pair, while higher temperature should pull the last peak just under 10 min. This tests whether a second distinct 1.000 method exists near the optimum.

With a perfect method already found, this nearby distinct run is to bracket robustness on the fast side. Shortening tG one step at the same successful phi window and temperature will show whether the critical 6/7 pair immediately drops below 1.5 or if an even shorter fully resolved method exists.

Since the critical 6/7 pair worsens when the gradient gets steeper, try a slightly lower phi0 at the successful phi1, tG, and T to shift the crowded mid-region to a shallower effective solvent ramp while keeping the last peak near 10 min. This may improve the weakest pair without sacrificing the fully resolved, on-time profile.

A perfect score is already achieved, so this is a robustness check around the optimum from the shallower-slope side. Increasing tG one step at the best phi window and temperature should further protect the critical 6/7 pair while likely only nudging the last peak slightly later.

The optimum is known, so this distinct run probes whether a slightly higher phi1 can offset the retention increase that came with narrowing to 0.55 while the higher temperature trims the tail. It is a robustness/selectivity check near the best region, especially for the temperature-sensitive 6/7 pair.

The perfect method at 0.15/0.55/8/40 suggests a narrow optimum, and changing phi0 downward slightly hurt the critical pair, so testing phi0 upward by one step maps the other side of that optimum. This checks whether the 6/7 pair improves or collapses when the same window is shifted later while keeping run time short.

Now that 0.20/0.55/8/40 also gives a perfect score, lower phi1 by one step to see whether the same shifted window can retain full resolution while keeping the last peak under 10 min. This maps the upper-edge robustness of the second optimum region.

The shifted optimum improved from phi0 0.15 to 0.20 at fixed phi1 0.55, so test one more step higher in phi0 to see whether the final peak can stay before 10 min while preserving the barely adequate 6/7 separation. This explores whether the second perfect region extends upward or if 0.20 is its upper edge.

Since 0.20/0.55/8/40 is perfect and lowering phi1 to 0.50 greatly delayed the last peak, test the other side by raising phi1 one step while keeping the successful higher phi0. This checks whether the 0.20 window is robust upward in phi1 or whether extra steepness will break the critical 6/7 pair.

Both perfect methods sit on a narrow selectivity ridge centered near 40 C, so this run tests whether the higher-phi0 optimum can tolerate a slightly shallower gradient if compensated by higher temperature. It is a distinct robustness check around the 0.20/0.55 window to see whether another practical maximum exists nearby.

We have mapped that 6/7 is strongly temperature-sensitive and also worsens when the gradient is made too steep at 40 C, but lower temperature shifts the troublesome pair identity in the 0.15/0.60 window. This run explores a distinct corner around the second optimum to see whether cooler temperature can stabilize selectivity enough to tolerate a faster 6 min method.

The 0.20/0.55/8/40 method is perfect, but we have not yet isolated whether temperature alone at this same window breaks a different pair as seen elsewhere at 35 C. Running the same optimum window at 35 C cleanly maps that selectivity effect around the second optimum.

We now know 35 C shifts the weak pair to 5/6, while 45 C in broader windows collapses 6/7; the missing point is temperature alone at the proven 0.20/0.55/8 window. This run completes the local temperature map around the second perfect method.

The center of the successful region is clear, but one remaining useful check is the diagonally opposite window from 0.20/0.55: lower phi0 and higher phi1 at the same tG and T. This tests whether the optimum follows a compensating window shift or is truly localized around phi1 0.55.

To complete the 2x2 window map around the lower-phi0 branch, test the missing combination with both phi0 and phi1 reduced. This will show whether narrowing the window at low phi0 can recover the weak 6/7 pair or if it mainly pushes the last peak too late, as seen elsewhere.

One unexplored check near the original 0.15 branch is whether increasing phi1 while keeping the successful phi0 and tG at 40 C creates a second fast local optimum or simply steepens enough to hurt 6/7. This fills the missing upper-phi1 point without confounding temperature.

The only nearby 40 C point still missing around the higher-phi0 branch is the upper-right corner at phi1 0.65. This tests whether increasing both phi0 and phi1 together preserves the compensating balance seen at 0.20/0.55 or over-steepens the critical 6/7 region.

For the final untried point nearest the successful high-phi0 branch, test whether raising both phi0 and phi1 together from 0.25/0.55 can rescue the early pair while keeping the later region workable. This completes the local map around the second optimum and checks if the failure at phi0 0.25 was mainly due to phi1 being too low.
